_: Every number here is derived from the plan's inputs by hand, from first
principles, NOT read out of a run of the application. That is the entire
point: the seven semantic sweeps prove the app agrees with itself and with a
recompute written after reading its source, which cannot catch an error that
was absorbed into both. These numbers can.

reading: This is the case the two measures disagree on, which is why the plan was built this way.
Against the spend curve the project is $3,500 UNDER — but only because D never started.
Against the value of the work actually finished it is $500 OVER.
A panel that reports only the first number calls a cost overrun a saving.

why: Bob really does work B (05-11 Mar) and C (05-06 Mar) at 100% each, so he
stands at 200% on Thursday 5 and Friday 6 March. A first-principles reading
The application reports zero, and it is right to: both B and C are 100%
complete, and its rule is that a conflict where all the overlapping work is
finished is history rather than an action item. You cannot un-double-book
a week that has already happened.
This entry exists to pin that rule down. It is a deliberate design decision
that a naive reading of 'over-allocated' does not predict, so it should be
asserted explicitly rather than discovered again later.

withCUnfinished.why: Set C to 0% complete and the same overlap becomes a live conflict: two (person x day) pairs, one person, two distinct dates.

theDisagreement: Three independent derivations, working from the written spec with no sight of
the implementation, all put E on 2026-03-17. Their argument is good: D's EF is
also 12 and D finishes 17 March, so dating E on the 18th makes one offset
resolve to two different calendar dates, and turns a 12-working-day plan into a
The application puts E on 2026-03-18, and does so deliberately: durationToDate()
adds one working day when the last thing in the plan is a milestone. Its reason
is also good, and it is about the world rather than the arithmetic — a sign-off
is an event somebody attends after the work is finished, not the instant the
work stops. Dating go-live on the same day the last build task ends would
promise a client something nobody does.
Both readings are defensible, so this is a CHOICE, and the choice is the app's
to make. What was not defensible was making it silently: the Analytics tab read
'12.0 days → finish Mar 18, 2026' with nothing between the two numbers, and a
reader counting working days off a calendar arrives at the 13th and concludes
So the convention stands and the fixture pins it, and the line now names the
extra day. This entry exists so the next person to derive 17 March from first
principles finds the reasoning instead of filing a bug.
milestoneDayConvention.theSpanIsOneLonger: and the panel must say so — asserted by the golden test

withoutTheMilestone.why: Remove E and the plan ends on D, a real activity: durationToDate(12) then gives 17 March and the span is 12 working days. The extra day is attached to the milestone, not to the number 12.
